answer.label: Not established as Michelangelo — an older artistic motto
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote rejects the Michelangelo credit and connects the motto with Giuntalodi’s imagery. Scholarship confirms that artistic connection; no individual coiner is established.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Renaissance motto associated with Giuntalodi; later Michelangelo attribution

Wikiquote traces erroneous Michelangelo attribution to Duppa 1806, while fetched Deswarte-Rosa 1988 article recounts Vasari’s description of Giuntalodi’s drawing with motto. Princeton catalog documents Blake engraving bearing Michelangelo attribution, not proof of authorship.
I am still learning: plain English gloss, not an identified historical translation

trail: Wikiquote explains why the Michelangelo credit is rejected. Attribution correction ↗
The scholarly article describes Giuntalodi’s drawing and motto without proving he invented the phrase. Art-historical evidence ↗
Princeton catalogs a later Blake engraving with Michelangelo’s name in its title. Later attribution artifact ↗
source.rightsNote: The short Italian motto is documented as a Renaissance inscription and in an engraving by William Blake, who died in 1827. The historical phrase predates 1931; the plain English gloss is supplied only to explain its meaning.

author.heading: About Anonymous
author.bio: The creator of this motto is not established by the checked evidence. It appears in an artistic tradition associated with Domenico Giuntalodi; that is different from proving that either Giuntalodi or Michelangelo coined it.
